definition: Synopsys Simpleware ScanIP is a 3D image processing and model generation software program developed by Synopsys Inc.
details: to visualise, analyse, quantify, segment and export 3D image data from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), microtomography and other modalities for computer-aided design (CAD), finite element analysis (FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and 3D printing. The software is used in the life sciences, materials science, nondestructive testing, reverse engineering and petrophysics. Segmented images can be exported in the STL file format, surface meshes and point clouds, to CAD and 3D printing or, with the FE module, exported as surface/volume meshes directly into leading computer-aided engineering (CAE) solvers. The CAD and NURBS add-on modules can be used to integrate CAD objects into image data, and to convert scan data into NURBS-based models for CAD. The SOLID, FLOW and LAPLACE add-on modules can be used to calculate effective material properties from scanned samples using homogenisation techniques. Since 2020, Simpleware software has included Simpleware AS Ortho and Simpleware AS Cardio, modules for automated segmentation of medical image data that uses artificial intelligence-based machine learning. explainer.lead: Synopsys Simpleware ScanIP is 3D image processing and model generation software developed by Synopsys Inc. It matters because it turns medical and industrial 3D scan data into models usable for design, simulation and printing.

tiers.eli5: It's a program that takes 3D pictures, like hospital scans, and helps you clean them up and turn them into solid models you can study or build.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to visualise, segment and export 3D image data from MRI, CT, microtomography and other modalities into formats for CAD, FEA, CFD and 3D printing. A pitfall is that segmentation quality drives everything downstream, since exported meshes and point clouds inherit its errors.
tiers.paperLevel: It is a commercial software package rather than an algorithm, so it has no formal definition or formula; its limits are those of the imaging modalities and export formats it supports.

explainer.example: A clinician segments a CT scan of a bone, then exports the segmented image as an STL file for 3D printing or as a surface mesh for finite element analysis.
